title: Exploring Student Behaviors and Motivations when using AI Teaching Assistants with Optional Guardrails
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students use an AI teaching assistant (AI TA) in introductory programming when the system includes optional guardrails. The core problem is a tension in AI-supported education: guardrails are intended to encourage learning by providing scaffolded help instead of direct answers, but if they are too restrictive, students may seek unmonitored solutions elsewhere or disable the restrictions. The study asks how often students choose to access direct AI-generated solutions, what motivates that choice, and how solution-seeking relates to course performance and timing of work.

To investigate this, the authors deployed a web-based tool called Edugator in one weekly lab of a large introductory programming course. The AI TA normally used prompt-based guardrails to avoid giving code solutions and instead provide conceptual help, but students could click a "See Solution" button to disable the guardrails and receive a verbatim response from the underlying model, including code. Students completed three C programming tasks (one code-writing task and two debugging tasks), while the researchers collected tool logs on chatbot use, solution-button clicks, submissions, and timing. The study also included an open-ended reflection question, which was analyzed thematically to understand students’ motivations for using or avoiding the solution feature.

The study involved 885 participating students from a single large public research university in the Australasian region during a 12-week Fall 2024 term, though data for this paper came from one lab activity spanning 9 days. Quantitative results showed that 50% of students used the "See Solution" feature at least once, and 14% used it for all three problems. Lower-performing students were more likely to use the feature for all tasks and were also more likely to work near the deadline. However, the decision to use the feature was not significantly associated with when students started the lab overall. Qualitative findings showed that students used the feature for problem-solving assistance, time pressure, lack of self-regulation, and curiosity, while those who avoided it often cited learning value, sufficient support from the guardrailed chatbot, or ethical concerns.

The paper concludes that optional access to unrestricted AI solutions reveals important student help-seeking behaviors that would otherwise be hidden if students simply turned to external tools. The authors argue that AI TA design should balance pedagogical safeguards with student preferences and needs, especially for struggling students who may be at greater risk of over-reliance. At the same time, the study does not establish causal effects on learning, and the authors recommend future work across longer periods and more controlled settings to determine when and for whom access to direct solutions may be beneficial or harmful.

identified_tools.name: Edugator
identified_tools.description: A web-based programming learning tool that lets instructors author problems, allows students to code in-browser, receive immediate feedback, and interact with an LLM-powered AI teaching assistant. In this study, the AI TA included optional guardrails and a 'See Solution' button that disabled those guardrails to generate a verbatim response from the underlying model.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in one lab of a large introductory programming course for three C programming tasks (one code-writing and two debugging tasks). Students could use the guardrailed AI TA for scaffolded help or click 'See Solution' to receive an unguarded LLM-generated solution/explanation; the study examined usage patterns, motivations, and associations with course performance.

findings.finding_summary: In the lab activity, 50% of the 885 participating students used the 'See Solution' feature at least once, while 50% did not use it. Specifically, 18% used it for one problem (n=160), 18% for two problems (n=158), and 14% for all three problems (n=122), showing substantial uptake of optional guardrail removal rather than a clearly beneficial or harmful academic effect.
findings.measure: Usage rate of the optional 'See Solution' feature across three programming tasks

findings.finding_summary: Students who used the 'See Solution' feature for all three problems had lower average scores on invigilated course tests (μ3=66) than students who never used it (μ0=73) or used it for one or two problems (μ1=72, μ2=73). The paper also reports that students in the lowest performance quartile were more likely to use the feature for all problems; for example, a student in Q1 was twice as likely to use it in all problems as a student in Q4.
findings.measure: Association between frequency of 'See Solution' use and invigilated exam performance / performance quartile

findings.finding_summary: Use of the 'See Solution' feature was not significantly related to when students started the lab. The authors report approximately 50% usage regardless of start date, with no significant differences between users and non-users by start date (χ²(7)=5.92, p=0.55), except that among students who started on the first available day, 65% did not use the feature.
findings.measure: Association between 'See Solution' usage and lab start date / timing

findings.finding_summary: Low-performing students interacted with the tool later and closer to the deadline than higher-performing students. The paper reports that 52% of submissions and 'See Solution' clicks by students in the lowest quartile (Q1) occurred within the last day before the assignment was due, and this deadline-proximate behavior decreased progressively from Q1 to Q4.
findings.measure: Timing of submissions and 'See Solution' clicks by student performance quartile

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative analysis of 839 non-blank reflections found mixed motivations for using or avoiding the optional unguarded solution feature. Students avoided it for perceived learning value, sufficient support from the guardrailed chatbot, or ethical concerns, while those who used it cited problem-solving assistance, time pressure, lack of self-regulation, and curiosity.
findings.measure: Student-reported motivations and help-seeking behavior from open-ended reflections

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI / GPT family model used here as the underlying LLM backend (the paper states OpenAI's 4o model).
identified_tools.use_case: Served as the underlying model powering Edugator's AI TA, including both the guardrailed scaffolded-help mode and the unguarded 'See Solution' mode that could generate detailed explanations and code solutions.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational mixed-methods study with log analysis and qualitative reflections, not a randomized or quasi-experimental design. Findings are correlational and the authors explicitly note they cannot determine causality.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful usage patterns and negative associations between heavy solution access and lower performance, but no causal impact estimates or standardized effect sizes. Overall educational impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.
